concept: Right-sizing Atlas tier from cache and CPU metrics
summary: Source-anchored research for Right-sizing Atlas tier from cache and CPU metrics. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Atlas treats M10 and M20 CPU thresholds differently because cloud providers can cap CPU after burst periods; their scale-down thresholds use provider-specific baseline CPU. A generic CPU p95 cutoff such as the one in the OneUptime guide should not be applied unchanged across tier families. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-19) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/cluster-autoscaling-compute-core/

Atlas Core reactive scale-down uses multiple signals across both 10-minute and 4-hour windows: operational nodes must average below 45% Normalized System CPU, below 90% of the maximum WiredTiger cache size, and below 60% Projected Memory Utilization at the new lower tier. Atlas's cost-saving guidance separately says to manually move to a lower tier by monitoring CPU, WiredTiger cache, memory, and IOPS over a rolling 30 day period of normal use. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/cluster-autoscaling-compute-core/ ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/architecture/current/cost-saving-config/

For manual right-sizing, Atlas recommends monitoring CPU, WiredTiger cache, memory, and IOPS over a rolling 30-day period of normal use; sustained use below 45% of allocated resources is a general signal to consider scaling down. A OneUptime guide recommends a two-week baseline, so that shorter window should be treated as practitioner advice rather than Atlas policy. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-21) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/architecture/current/cost-saving-config/ ; https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-03-31-mongodb-right-size-atlas-clusters/view

Cache hit rate is not a safe standalone tier gate. MongoDB says the working set does not have to fit entirely in RAM because WiredTiger evicts pages and the OS filesystem cache can hold compressed data. Guy Harrison also notes that a high cache hit ratio can coexist with an inefficient workload that repeatedly reads the same blocks. Atlas scale-down checks use cache occupancy and projected memory rather than a cache hit-rate threshold. (medium confidence) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/faq/diagnostics/ ; https://web.archive.org/web/2024/https://medium.com/mongodb-performance-tuning/the-notorious-database-cache-hit-ratio-c7d432381229 ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/cluster-autoscaling-compute-core/

Assess WiredTiger cache pressure with multiple signals instead of cache occupancy alone. Atlas exposes cache fill and dirty fill ratios alongside disk IOPS and latency. Percona's guidance says that if pages read into cache is consistently a large part of the cache size, memory is under pressure and more memory may improve read performance, and that a high rate of dirty pages can affect query performance. Check query latency and I/O before downsizing, even when CPU is low. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/review-available-metrics/ ; https://www.percona.com/blog/mongodb-101-how-to-tune-your-mongodb-configuration-after-upgrading-to-more-memory/ ; https://www.percona.com/blog/percona-monitoring-and-management-pmm-graphs-explained-wiredtiger-and-percona-memory-engine/

A candidate tier must also fit workload limits beyond CPU and cache: Atlas says the number of client connections a cluster supports is determined by its cluster tier, network bandwidth is faster at higher tiers, and the Atlas metrics page advises monitoring whether disk IOPS approaches the maximum provisioned IOPS. Check those constraints before selecting the smaller tier. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/sizing-tier-selection/ ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/review-available-metrics/

Treat a tier reduction as a measured change with a rollback path. MyDBOps recommends a 30-day CPU, memory, and IOPS baseline and remeasurement after resizing; OneUptime suggests a 14-day baseline and post-change monitoring. These are practitioner recommendations with different windows, so neither duration nor its suggested CPU cutoff is a universal safety guarantee. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-08-07) Sources: https://www.mydbops.com/blog/how-to-reduce-mongodb-atlas-costs-at-scale ; https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-03-31-mongodb-right-size-atlas-clusters/view
